:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Classifying a System as Consistent Dependent, Consistent Independent, or Inconsistent

:question/answer-fields.:answer-field/key: The system has a unique solution

questions.:question/problem:
Consider the following system of equations.

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x-y+z &=3 \\ -3x+3y-3z &=10\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.
questions.:question/worked-solution:
To classify the system, we first need to find its solution. The augmented matrix for this system is

$$
M=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 1 & 3 \\ -3 & 3 & -3 & 10\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Using the method of Gaussian elimination, we can reduce this matrix to row echelon form as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 1 & 3 \\ -3 & 3 & -3 & 10\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 1 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 19\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The final row corresponds to the equation $0x+0y+0z=19,$ and this has no solution. Therefore, our system has no solution, and we conclude that the system is inconsistent.

As a result, only statement “The system is inconsistent” is true.

$$

To classify the system, we first need to find its solution. The augmented matrix for this system is

$$
M=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 2 \\ -3 & -4 & 3 \\ 2 & -4 & -1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Using the method of Gaussian elimination, we can reduce this matrix to row echelon form as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 2 \\ -3 & -4 & 3 \\ 2 & -4 & -1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 2 \\ 0 & -10 & 9 \\ 2 & -4 & -1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 2 \\ 0 & -10 & 9 \\ 0 & 0 & -5\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The final row corresponds to the equation $0x+0y=-5,$ and this has no solution. Therefore, our system has no solution, and we conclude that the system is inconsistent.

As a result, only statement “The system is inconsistent” is true.

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Identifying Steady-State Vectors of Stochastic Matrices

questions.:question/problem:
$$
P=\begin{bmatrix}0.8 & 0.15 \\ 0.2 & 0.85\end{bmatrix},\,q=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{3}{7} \\ \frac{4}{7}\end{bmatrix}
$$

Consider the stochastic matrix $P$ and vector $q$ shown above. Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.
questions.:question/worked-solution:
Recall that a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix $P$ is a stochastic vector $q$ such that $Pq=q.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement “$q$ is a stochastic vector” is true. Indeed, $q$ is a stochastic vector since its entries are non-negative and add up to $1.$

- Statement $Pq=q$ is true. Indeed, we have 

$$
Pq=\begin{bmatrix}0.8 & 0.15 \\ 0.2 & 0.85\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{3}{7} \\ \frac{4}{7}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{2.4}{7}+\frac{0.6}{7} \\ \frac{0.6}{7}+\frac{3.4}{7}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{3}{7} \\ \frac{4}{7}\end{bmatrix}=q.
$$

- Statement “$q$ is a steady-state vector of $P$” is true. Indeed, $q$ is a stochastic vector such that $Pq=q.$ So, it's a steady-state vector of $P.$

Therefore, the correct answer is “$q$ is a stochastic vector”; $Pq=q$; “$q$ is a steady-state vector of $P$”.

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Identifying True Statements About the Dot Product

questions.:question/problem:
Suppose $a\cdot (a+b)=0$, where $a\ne 0.$ Which of the following statements are true? 

Select all that apply.
questions.:question/worked-solution:
Let's analyze each statement in turn.

- Statement $a\cdot a<0$ is false. Indeed, $a\ne 0$ implies that $a\cdot a>0.$

- Statement $b\cdot a>0$ and $b\cdot a=5$ are false. Simplifying the expression $a\cdot (a+b)=0$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}a\cdot (a+b) & =0 \\ a\cdot a+a\cdot b & =0 \\ a\cdot a+b\cdot a & =0 \\ b\cdot a & =-a\cdot a\end{aligned}
$$

 
Since $a\ne 0$ implies that $a\cdot a>0$, we obtain that $b\cdot a<0.$

Therefore, we conclude that the correct answer is "None of the statements are true".

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Identifying the Reasons Why a Determinant Equals Zero

questions.:question/problem:
Let $A$ be a $2\times 2$ matrix such that $|A|\ne 0.$ Which of the following statements must be true?

Select all that apply.
questions.:question/worked-solution:
Let's consider our statements in turn.

- Statement “$A$ is a triangular matrix” is false. For example, consider the matrix 

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

We have that 

$$
|A|=1\cdot 1-(-2)\cdot 2=5\ne 0
$$

but $A$ is not a triangular matrix.

- Statements “$A$ does not have identical rows” and “$A$ does not have proportional columns” are true. Indeed, we can make use of the following fact:

$|A|=0$ *if and only if one of the rows/columns of $A$ is a linear combination of other rows/columns of $A.$*

In the case of a $2\times 2$ matrix, this means that one of the rows/columns must be proportional to another row/column.
Hence, if $|A|\ne 0$ then $A$ doesn't have proportional nor identical rows/columns.

Therefore, the correct answer is “$A$ does not have identical rows”; “$A$ does not have proportional columns” only.

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Identifying True Statements About Orthogonal Vectors in Inner Product Spaces

:question/answer-fields.:answer-field/key: $f(t)⊥g(t)$ with respect to the inner product $⟨\cdot ,\cdot ⟩$ in $V$

questions.:question/problem:
Let $V=C[-1,0]$ be the vector space of all functions that are continuous on $[-1,0],$ equipped with the inner product 

$$
⟨f(t),g(t)⟩={\int }_{-1}^{0}f(t)g(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Given the functions $f(t)=({t}^{3}+t+1)^{3}$ and $g(t)=3{t}^{2}+1,$ which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.
questions.:question/worked-solution:
First, we need to evaluate 

$$
⟨f(t),g(t)⟩={\int }_{-1}^{0}({t}^{3}+t+1)^{3}(3{t}^{2}+1)\,\text{d}t.
$$

We can evaluate this integral using the substitution $u={t}^{3}+t+1,$ $\text{d}u=(3{t}^{2}+1)\,\text{d}t$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{0}({t}^{3}+t+1)^{3}(3{t}^{2}+1)\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{u}^{3}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{u}^{4}\,{|}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =[\frac{1}{4}(1)^{4}]-[\frac{1}{4}(-1)^{4}] \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Let's now examine the statements:

- Statement $⟨f(t),g(t)⟩=0$ is true, while statement $⟨f(t),g(t)⟩=\frac{1}{4}$ is false. This is as a result of the above calculations.

- Statement “$f(t)⊥g(t)$ with respect to the inner product $⟨\cdot ,\cdot ⟩$ in $V$” is true. Since the inner product is zero, our vectors are orthogonal.

Therefore, the correct answer is $⟨f(t),g(t)⟩=0$; “$f(t)⊥g(t)$ with respect to the inner product $⟨\cdot ,\cdot ⟩$ in $V$” only.

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Determining Whether a Set of Functions is Orthogonal With Respect to a Given Inner Product

:question/answer-fields.:answer-field/key: ${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product
${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product
$S=\{{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t),{f}_{3}(t)\}$ is an orthogonal set with respect to the given inner product

questions.:question/problem:
Consider the following set of functions:

$$
{f}_{1}(t)=t,\,{f}_{2}(t)={e}^{t},\,{f}_{3}(t)={e}^{-t}
$$

Given that the inner product in the vector space $C[-1,1]$ of continuous functions over $[-1,1]$ is defined as 

$$
⟨f(t),g(t)⟩={\int }_{-1}^{1}f(t)g(t)\,\text{d}t,
$$

which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.
questions.:question/worked-solution:
Recall that a set of vectors in an inner product space is called orthogonal if all vectors in the set are mutually orthogonal with respect to the given inner product. 

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement “${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product” is false. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩ & =⟨t,{e}^{t}⟩ \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}t{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Let's use integration by parts. We denote

$$
\begin{aligned}u=t & ⟹ & {u}^{′}=1, \\ {v}^{′}={e}^{t} & ⟹ & v=\int {v}^{′}\,\text{d}t=\int {e}^{t}\,\text{d}t={e}^{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, applying the integration by parts formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{1}t{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t & =uv{|}_{-1}^{1}-{\int }_{-1}^{1}{u}^{′}v\,\text{d}t \\  & =t{e}^{t}{|}_{-1}^{1}-{\int }_{-1}^{1}{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =(e+{e}^{-1})-{e}^{t}{|}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =(e+{e}^{-1})-(e-{e}^{-1}) \\  & =2{e}^{-1}\ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that ${f}_{1}(t)⊥̸{f}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement “${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product” is false. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{3}(t)⟩ & =⟨t,{e}^{-t}⟩ \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}t{e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Let's use integration by parts. We denote

$$
\begin{aligned}u=t & ⟹ & {u}^{′}=1, \\ {v}^{′}={e}^{-t} & ⟹ & v=\int {v}^{′}\,\text{d}t=\int {e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t=-{e}^{-t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, applying the integration by parts formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{1}t{e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t & =uv{|}_{-1}^{1}-{\int }_{-1}^{1}{u}^{′}v\,\text{d}t \\  & =-t{e}^{-t}{|}_{-1}^{1}+{\int }_{-1}^{1}{e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =(-{e}^{-1}-e)-{e}^{-t}{|}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =(-{e}^{-1}-e)-({e}^{-1}-e) \\  & =-2{e}^{-1}\ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that ${f}_{1}(t)⊥̸{f}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement “$S=\{{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t),{f}_{3}(t)\}$ is an orthogonal set with respect to the given inner product” is false. Since ${f}_{1}(t)⊥̸{f}_{2}(t),$ the set $S$ is *not* orthogonal.

Therefore, the correct answer is "None of the statements are true."

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Identifying True Statements About Orthogonal Matrices

:question/answer-fields.:answer-field/key: If $\lambda $ is a real eigenvalue of $Q,$ then $\lambda =\pm 1$
If the determinant of $P$ is either $1$ or $-1,$ then $P$ is orthogonal

questions.:question/problem:
Which of the following statements are true regarding the $n\times n$ orthogonal matrix $Q$ and the $n\times n$ matrix $P?$

Select all that apply.
questions.:question/worked-solution:
Recall that a matrix $Q$ is orthogonal if and only if

$$
Q{Q}^{T}={Q}^{T}Q=I.
$$

To check that a matrix is orthogonal, it is sufficient to check that the above equation is satisfied.

Moreover, we have the following properties:

- For any orthogonal matrix $Q,$ we have ${Q}^{-1}={Q}^{T}.$

- $(AB)^{T}={B}^{T}{A}^{T}$ for conformable matrices $A$ and $B.$

With that in mind, let's inspect each of the statements in turn.

- Statement “If $\lambda $ is a real eigenvalue of $Q,$ then $\lambda =\pm 1$” is true. If $\lambda $ is an eigenvalue of an orthogonal matrix $Q$ then $\lambda =\pm 1$

- Statement “If the determinant of $P$ is either $1$ or $-1,$ then $P$ is orthogonal” is false. Every orthogonal matrix has the determinant equal to $\pm 1$, but not every matrix with the determinant equal to $\pm 1$ is orthogonal. As a counterexample, consider the following matrix:

$$
P=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

The determinant of $P$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}det(P)=2\cdot 1-1\cdot 1=1,\end{aligned}
$$

 however, $P$ is not orthogonal since, for example, the first column is not normalized.

- Statement “$Q-I$ is singular” is false. As a counterexample, consider the following orthogonal matrix:

$$
Q=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{3}{5} & -\frac{4}{5} \\ \frac{4}{5} & \frac{3}{5}\end{bmatrix}
$$

We have that

$$
Q-I=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{3}{5} & -\frac{4}{5} \\ \frac{4}{5} & \frac{3}{5}\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{2}{5} & -\frac{4}{5} \\ \frac{4}{5} & -\frac{2}{5}\end{bmatrix}
$$

and $Q-I$ is not singular since, for example, it doesn't have proportional rows or columns.

Therefore, the correct answer is “If $\lambda $ is a real eigenvalue of $Q,$ then $\lambda =\pm 1$” only.

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Verifying Continuity of Three-Piece Functions

questions.:question/problem:
Which of the following statements are true regarding the function $g(x),$ defined below?

$$
g(x)={\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{x-1}, & x<0 \\ -1, & x=0 \\ x+1, & x>0\end{aligned}
$$

Select all that apply.
questions.:question/worked-solution:
We're required to determine the left and right continuity properties of $g(x)$ at $x=0.$

First, we note that 

$$
\begin{aligned}g(0)=-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's look at each statement in turn:

- Statement “$g(x)$ is left-continuous at $x=0$” is true. The function is left-continuous at $x=0$ since the left-sided limit is equal to the function value:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {0}^{-}}g(x) & =\frac{1}{0-1} \\  & =-\frac{1}{1} \\  & =-1 \\  & =g(0)\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement “$g(x)$ is right-continuous at $x=0$” is false. The function is *not* right-continuous at $x=0$ since the right-sided limit is *not* equal to the function value:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}g(x) & =0+1 \\  & =1 \\  & \ne g(0)\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement “$g(x)$ is continuous at $x=0$” is false. For the function to be continuous at $x=0,$ it must be both left-continuous and right-continuous. However, we have already determined that the function is not right-continuous at $x=0.$

Therefore, the correct answer is “$g(x)$ is left-continuous at $x=0$” only.

questions.:question/problem:

questions.:question/worked-solution:
We're required to determine the left and right continuity properties of $h(x)$ at $x=\frac{\pi }{2}.$

First, we note that 

$$
\begin{aligned}h\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's look at each statement in turn:

- Statement “$h(x)$ is left-continuous at $x=\frac{\pi }{2}$” is false. The function is *not* left-continuous at $x=\frac{\pi }{2}$ since the left-sided limit is *not* equal to the function value:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (\pi /2)^{-}}h(x) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right) \\  & =0 \\  & \ne h\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement “$h(x)$ is right-continuous at $x=\frac{\pi }{2}$” is false. The function is *not* right-continuous at $x=\frac{\pi }{2}$ since the right-sided limit is *not* equal to the function value:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (\pi /2)^{+}}h(x) & =2\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right) \\  & =\pi  \\  & \ne h\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement “$h(x)$ is continuous at $x=\frac{\pi }{2}$” is false. For the function to be continuous at $x=\frac{\pi }{2},$ it must be both left-continuous and right-continuous. However, we have already determined that the function is neither left-continuous nor right-continuous at $x=\frac{\pi }{2}.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "None."

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Identifying a Solution to a First-Order Differential Equation

:question/answer-fields.:answer-field/key: Substituting $y=f(x)$ and ${y}^{′}={f}^{′}(x)$ into the differential equation gives a true statement
The function $y=f(x)$ is a solution of the differential equation

questions.:question/problem:
Consider the following differential equation.

$$
{y}^{′}=2y
$$

Let $f(x)=\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2x.$ Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.
questions.:question/worked-solution:
For a function $f(x)$ to be a solution to a differential equation, it must satisfy the equation for all values of $x$ in the equation's domain.

With that in mind, let's check each statement in turn.

- Statement ${f}^{′}(x)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡2x$ is false. Differentiating $f(x)=\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2x,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & ={(\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2x)}^{′} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 2\operatorname{cos}⁡2x \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡2x \\  & \ne 2\operatorname{cos}⁡2x.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement “Substituting $y=f(x)$ and ${y}^{′}={f}^{′}(x)$ into the differential equation gives a true statement” is false. Substituting $y=\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2x$ and ${y}^{′}=\operatorname{cos}⁡2x$ into the original equation, we get a false statement:

$$

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Identifying Closure Properties of Polynomials

questions.:question/problem:
Which of the following expressions are polynomials?

Select all that apply.
questions.:question/worked-solution:
Recall that polynomials have the following closure properties:

- Polynomials are closed under addition, subtraction, and multiplication. This means that the sum, difference, and product of two polynomials is *always* a polynomial.

- Polynomials are *not* closed under division. This means that the quotient of two polynomials is *not* always a polynomial.

With that in mind, let's examine our expressions in turn.

- Expression $(4{x}^{6}-2)÷(2x)$ is *not* a polynomial. Carrying out the division, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{4{x}^{6}-2}{2x} & =\frac{4{x}^{6}}{2x}-\frac{2}{2x} \\  & =2{x}^{5}-\frac{1}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

which is *not* a polynomial.

- Expression $(7x+1)\cdot (2{x}^{3}+3)$ gives a polynomial. It's a product of two polynomials, and polynomials are closed under multiplication.

- Expression $({x}^{4}-3{x}^{2}+1)÷({x}^{2})$ is *not* a polynomial. Carrying out the division, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{4}-3{x}^{2}+1}{{x}^{2}} & =\frac{{x}^{4}}{{x}^{2}}-\frac{3{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}}+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}} \\  & ={x}^{2}-3+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

which is *not* a polynomial.

Therefore, the correct answer is $(7x+1)\cdot (2{x}^{3}+3)$ only.

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Identifying True Statements Using the Invertible Matrix Theorem

questions.:question/problem:
Which of the following statements are true, given that $A$ is a $5\times 5$ matrix and 

$$
\text{Null}(A)=\left\{\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ 0 \\ 2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{1}\end{bmatrix}\,|\,{x}_{1},{x}_{2}\in R\right\}?
$$

Select all that apply.
questions.:question/worked-solution:
Since $A$ is a $5\times 5$ matrix, the invertible matrix theorem states the following:

$$
A\text{ is }\text{invertible}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\left\{\begin{aligned}\operatorname{Col}(A) &=\mathbb{R}^{5} \\ \dim(\operatorname{Col}(A)) &=5=\operatorname{rank}(A) \\ \operatorname{Null}(A) &=\{0\} \\ \dim(\operatorname{Null}(A)) &=0=\operatorname{nullity}(A)\end{aligned}\right.
$$

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn.

- Statement $\text{dim(Null}(A))=0$ is false. Since 

$$
\text{Null}(A)=\left\{{x}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1 \\ 0 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\,|\,{x}_{1},{x}_{2}\in R\right\}
$$

we conclude that 

$$
\text{dim(Null}(A))=2\ne 0.
$$

- Statement “$A$ is  invertible” is false. Since $\text{dim(Null}(A))\ne 0,$ then according to the invertible matrix theorem, the matrix $A$ can't be invertible.

- Statement $\text{Col}(A)\ne {R}^{5}$ is true. Since $A$ is not invertible, then by the invertible matrix theorem, we must have $\text{Col}(A)\ne {R}^{5}.$

Therefore, the correct answer is $\text{Col}(A)\ne {R}^{5}$ only.

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Determining Whether Two Random Variables are Independent Given the Joint PMF Only

questions.:question/problem:
The joint probability distribution $f(x,y)$ of the discrete random variables $X$ and $Y$ is given below. 

| $f$ | $Y=1$ | $Y=2$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $X=1$ | $0.6$ | $0.2$ |
| $X=2$ | $0.15$ | $0.05$ |

Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.
questions.:question/worked-solution:
Two discrete random variables $X$ and $Y$ with a joint probability mass function $f(x,y)$ are independent if and only if 

$$
f(x,y)={f}_{X}(x)\cdot {f}_{Y}(y)
$$

 

for all possible values $x$ and $y,$ where ${f}_{X}(x)$ and ${f}_{Y}(y)$ are the marginal probability mass functions for $X$ and $Y,$ respectively.

Computing the marginal probability mass functions for  $X$ and $Y,$ we obtain the following:

| $f$ | $Y=1$ | $Y=2$ | ${f}_{X}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $X=1$ | $0.6$ | $0.2$ | $0.8$ |
| $X=2$ | $0.15$ | $0.05$ | $0.2$ |
| ${f}_{Y}$ | $0.75$ | $0.25$ | $1$ |

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement $P(X=2,Y=1)$ $=P(X=2)\cdot P(Y=1)$ is true. From the table, we obtain that $P(X=2,Y=1)=f(2,1)=0.15.$ On the other hand, 

$$
P(X=2)\cdot P(Y=1)={f}_{X}(2)\cdot {f}_{Y}(1)=0.2\cdot 0.75=0.15.\,✓
$$

- Statement “$P(X=x,Y=y)$ $=P(X=x)\cdot P(Y=y)$ for all possible $x$ and $y$” is true. Checking all other possible products, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1,1) & =0.6=0.8\cdot 0.75={f}_{X}(1)\cdot {f}_{Y}(1) & ✓ \\ f(1,2) & =0.2=0.8\cdot 0.25={f}_{X}(1)\cdot {f}_{Y}(2) & ✓ \\ f(2,2) & =0.05=0.2\cdot 0.25={f}_{X}(2)\cdot {f}_{Y}(2) & ✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, $P(X=x,Y=y)$ $=P(X=x)\cdot P(Y=y)$ for all possible $x$ and $y.$

- Statement “$X$ and $Y$ are independent” is true. Since statement “$P(X=x,Y=y)$ $=P(X=x)\cdot P(Y=y)$ for all possible $x$ and $y$” is true, our random variables $X$ and $Y$ must be independent.

Therefore, the correct answer is $P(X=2,Y=1)$ $=P(X=2)\cdot P(Y=1)$; “$P(X=x,Y=y)$ $=P(X=x)\cdot P(Y=y)$ for all possible $x$ and $y$”; “$X$ and $Y$ are independent”.

questions.:question/problem:
Which of the following statements are true regarding the function $h(x),$ defined below?

$$
h(x)={\begin{aligned}-\sqrt{-x}, & x\le -1 \\ 1-2x, & x>-1\end{aligned}
$$

Select all that apply.
questions.:question/worked-solution:
We're required to determine the left and right continuity properties of $h(x)$ at $x=-1.$

Let's start by computing $h(-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}h(-1) & =-\sqrt{-(-1)} \\  & =-\sqrt{1} \\  & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's look at each statement in turn:

- Statement “$h(x)$ is left-continuous at $x=-1$” is true. The function is left-continuous at $x=-1$ since the left-sided limit is equal to the function value:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (-1)^{-}}h(x) & =-\sqrt{-(-1)} \\  & =-\sqrt{1} \\  & =-1 \\  & =h(-1)\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement “$h(x)$ is right-continuous at $x=-1$” is false. The function is *not* right-continuous at $x=-1$ since the right-sided limit is *not* equal to the function value:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (-1)^{+}}h(x) & =1-2(-1) \\  & =1+2 \\  & =3 \\  & \ne h(-1)\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement “$h(x)$ is continuous at $x=-1$” is false. For the function to be continuous at $x=-1,$ it must be both left-continuous and right-continuous. However, we have already determined that the function is not right-continuous at $x=-1.$

Therefore, the correct answer is “$h(x)$ is left-continuous at $x=-1$” only.

questions.:question/problem:
Consider the following function:

$$
f(x)={\begin{aligned}-4-x, & x\le 2 \\ -3x, & x>2\end{aligned}

questions.:question/worked-solution:
To test for continuity of $f(x)$ at a point $x=c$, we need to check three conditions:

- Does $f(c)$ exist?

- Does ${lim}_{x\to c}f(x)$ exist?

- Does ${lim}_{x\to c}f(x)=f(c)?$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement “$f(x)$ is defined at $x=2$” is true. Using the expression for the first branch of the function, we obtain that 

$$
f(2)=-4-2=-6.
$$

So, $f(x)$ is defined at $x=2.$ $\,\,✓$

- Statement ${lim}_{x\to {2}^{-}}f(x)={lim}_{x\to {2}^{+}}f(x)$ is true. By calculating the one-sided limits, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {2}^{-}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {2}^{-}}(-4-x) \\  & =-4-2 \\  & =-6 \\ {lim}_{x\to {2}^{+}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {2}^{+}}(-3x) \\  & =-3(2) \\  & =-6\end{aligned}
$$

As a result:

$$
{lim}_{x\to {2}^{-}}f(x)={lim}_{x\to {2}^{+}}f(x)
$$

 
Therefore, the limit of $f(x)$ at $x=2$ exists:

$$
{lim}_{x\to 2}f(x)=-6\,\,✓
$$

- Statement ${lim}_{x\to 2}f(x)=f(2)$ is true. Indeed, we have that ${lim}_{x\to 2}f(x)=-6=f(2).$  $\,\,✓$

- Statement “$f(x)$ has a discontinuity at $x=2$” is false. Since all statements “$f(x)$ is defined at $x=2$”; ${lim}_{x\to {2}^{-}}f(x)={lim}_{x\to {2}^{+}}f(x)$; ${lim}_{x\to 2}f(x)=f(2)$ are true, according to the continuity test, the function $f(x)$ is continuous at $x=2.$

Therefore, the correct answer is “$f(x)$ is defined at $x=2$”; ${lim}_{x\to {2}^{-}}f(x)={lim}_{x\to {2}^{+}}f(x)$; ${lim}_{x\to 2}f(x)=f(2)$ only.

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Determining Whether a Line Is a Subspace of Three-Dimensional Space

questions.:question/problem:
Let $L$ be the line in ${R}^{3}$ that passes through the points $(1,1,1)$ and $(2,-1,2).$ Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.
questions.:question/worked-solution:
Recall the following two facts about subspaces: 

- A set of vectors in a vector space is a *subspace* if it is closed under vector addition and scalar multiplication.

- If a non-empty set is closed under scalar multiplication, then this set must contain the zero-vector (because $0\cdot v=0$ for any vector $v$). So, if a set does not contain the zero vector, then this set is not closed under scalar multiplication.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements. 

- Statement “$L$ contains the zero-vector” is false. The direction vector of the line $L$ is 

$$
d=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

This means that the vector equation of the line is

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}+t\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

for $t\in R,$ and the corresponding Cartesian equation is 

$$
x-1=\frac{y-1}{-2}=z-1.
$$

But this line does not pass through the origin since 

$$
(0)-1\ne \frac{(0)-1}{-2}\ne (0)-1.\,\times 
$$

- Statement “$L$ is closed under vector addition” is false. Let's consider the vectors $\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}$ and $\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}$ from $L$ (the position vectors of the given points). Then,

$$
\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 0 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}.
$$

However, the point $(3,0,3)$ does not belong to $L$ since

$$
(3)-1\ne \frac{(0)-1}{-2}\ne (3)-1.\,\times 
$$

- Statement “$L$ is closed under scalar multiplication” is false. Since $0\notin L,$ this set is not closed under scalar multiplication.

- Statement “$L$ is a subspace of ${R}^{3}$” is false. Since statements “$L$ is closed under vector addition” and “$L$ is closed under scalar multiplication” are false, $L$ is *not* a subspace of ${R}^{3}.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "None of the statements are true."

- Statement “$L$ is closed under scalar multiplication” is false. Since $0\notin L,$ this set is not closed under scalar multiplication.

- Statement “$L$ is a subspace of ${R}^{3}$” is false. Since statements “$L$ is closed under vector addition” and “$L$ is closed under scalar multiplication” are false, $L$ is *not* a subspace of ${R}^{3}.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "None of the statements are true."

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Determining Whether a Plane Is a Subspace of Three-Dimensional Space

questions.:question/problem:
Let $Π$ be the plane with equation $x-2y+2z=3$ in ${R}^{3}.$ Which of the following statements are true? 

Select all that apply.
questions.:question/worked-solution:
Recall the following two facts about subspaces: 

- A set of vectors in a vector space is a *subspace* if it is closed under vector addition and scalar multiplication.

- If a non-empty set is closed under scalar multiplication, then this set must contain the zero-vector (because $0\cdot v=0$ for any vector $v$). So, if a set does not contain the zero vector, then this set is not closed under scalar multiplication.

Notice that $Π$ contains vectors of the form 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}3+2y-2z \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix},\,y,z\in R.
$$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements. 

- Statement “$Π$ contains the zero-vector” is false. The line does not pass through the origin since

$$
\begin{aligned}x-2y+2z & =3 \\ (0)-2(0)+2(0) & =3 \\ 0 & =3\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

- Statement “$Π$ is closed under vector addition” is false. Let's consider $a=\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\in Π$ and $b=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\in Π.$ Then 

$$
\begin{aligned}a+b & =\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}3+1 \\ 0+0 \\ 0+1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

However, $\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}$ does not belong to $Π$ since 

$$
\begin{aligned}x-2y+2z & =3 \\ (4)-2(0)+2(1) & =3 \\ 6 & =3\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

- Statement “$Π$ is closed under scalar multiplication” is false. Since $0\notin Π,$ this set is not closed under scalar multiplication.

- Statement “$Π$ is a subspace of ${R}^{3}$” is false. Since statements “$Π$ is closed under vector addition” and “$Π$ is closed under scalar multiplication” are false, $L$ is *not* a subspace of ${R}^{3}.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "None of the statements are true."

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Checking Whether a Given Function Is a Valid PDF

:question/answer-fields.:answer-field/key: $f(x)$ is a valid probability density function

questions.:question/problem:
$$
f(x)={\begin{aligned}{e}^{x/2},\, & x\le 0, \\ 0,\, & \text{otherwise.}\end{aligned}
$$

Given the function $f(x)$ above, which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.
questions.:question/worked-solution:
For a function $f(x)$ to be a valid probability density function on a set $S,$ it must satisfy the following conditions:

- $f(x)\ge 0$ for all $x\in S$

- ${\int }_{S}f(x)\,\text{d}x=1$

Now, let's consider each statement in turn:

- Statement “$f(x)\ge 0$ for all $x\le 0$” is true. Indeed, for $x\le 0,$ we have $f(x)={e}^{x/2}\ge 0.$

- Statement ${\int }_{-\infty }^{0}f(x)\,\text{d}x=1$ is false. Indeed,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}f(x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}{e}^{x/2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2{e}^{x/2}\,{|}_{-\infty }^{0} \\  & =2({e}^{0}-0) \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement “$f(x)$ is a valid probability density function” is false. Since statement ${\int }_{-\infty }^{0}f(x)\,\text{d}x=1$ is false, $f(x)$ is not a valid probability density function.

Therefore, the correct answer is “$f(x)\ge 0$ for all $x\le 0$” only.

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Finding the Image of a Horizontal Segment Under a Polar Transformation

:question/answer-fields.:answer-field/key: The image makes the angle of $0$ with the positive $x$-axis.
The image makes the angle of $\frac{3\pi }{4}$ with the positive $x$-axis.
One endpoint of the image is the origin $O$ of the $xy$-plane, and the other endpoint lies on the circle of radius $5$ centered at $O.$

questions.:question/problem:
![](images/8a/8afe0884ccf1e62ffdfef6cab4626bc59b3138aa5cd26f855980c88971753447.png)

Consider the square region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane, given by

$$
Δ={(u,v)\,:\,0\le u\le \sqrt{5},\,\,0\le v\le \frac{3\pi }{4}},
$$

and the transformation $T,$ given by

$$
T:(u,v)\to (u\operatorname{cos}⁡v,\,u\operatorname{sin}⁡v).
$$

The image of the top side of $Δ$ under the action of $T$ is a line segment. Which of the following statements are true regarding the image?

Select all that apply.
questions.:question/worked-solution:
To map the entire region $Δ$ onto the $xy$-plane, we consider the transformation of each side. However, in this case, we consider only the top side.

For the top side, we have $v=\frac{3\pi }{4}$ and $0\le u\le \sqrt{5}.$ 

Substituting $v=\frac{3\pi }{4}$ into our transformation equations, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(x,y) & =T(u,v) \\  & =(u\operatorname{cos}⁡v,\,u\operatorname{sin}⁡v) \\  & =(u\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{3\pi }{4}\right),\,u\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{3\pi }{4}\right)),\,0\le u\le \sqrt{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

This is a parametric equation of the line segment shown below.

![](images/b8/b836799bc512db70d2ce5fcfe70db2af3b2572d584d317fa5ed515b363a11ddc.png)

 

Note that the line that this segment lies on passes through the origin. 

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement “The image makes the angle of $0$ with the positive $x$-axis” is false, while statement “The image makes the angle of $\frac{3\pi }{4}$ with the positive $x$-axis” is true. The slope of the line is

$$
k=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{3\pi }{4}\right)}{\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{3\pi }{4}\right)}=\operatorname{tan}⁡\left(\frac{3\pi }{4}\right).
$$

As a result, our line makes an angle of $\frac{3\pi }{4}$ radians with the positive $x$-axis.

- Statement “One endpoint of the image is the origin $O$ of the $xy$-plane, and the other endpoint lies on the circle of radius $5$ centered at $O.$” is false.

- When $u=0,$ we obtain the point $(0,\,0),$ which is the origin $O$ of the $xy$-plane.

- When $u=\sqrt{5},$ we obtain the point 
$(\sqrt{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{3\pi }{4}\right),\,\sqrt{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{3\pi }{4}\right)),$
whose distance to $O$ is $\sqrt{5}.$

So, one endpoint of the segment is the origin $O$ of the $xy$-plane, while the other endpoint lies in the circle with radius $\sqrt{5}$ centered at $O.$

Therefore, the correct answer is “The image makes the angle of $\frac{3\pi }{4}$ with the positive $x$-axis” only.

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Identifying True Statements Regarding Interiors and Boundaries of Sets

:question/answer-fields.:answer-field/key: $A$ contains none of its boundary points.

questions.:question/problem:
Consider the set $A,$ defined by 

$$
A=\{(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,y\ge 2-x\}.
$$

Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.
questions.:question/worked-solution:
The boundary of a set $A,$ denoted $∂A,$ is the set that contains all the boundary points of $A.$

In this case, the set $A$ and its boundary $∂A$ are shown below.

![](images/cd/cdca164d343d8bff4c78a1e366e52c588ca6c54dfdea61acea1900bcbdc79f31.png)

The interior of a set $A,$ denoted $\text{int}\,A,$ is the set containing all the interior points of $A.$ It contains every point in $A$ except the boundary points: 

$$
\text{int}\,A=A-∂A
$$

Notice that, in this case, the set $A$ contains all of its boundary points.

With that in mind, let's examine each statement:

- Statements “$A$ contains none of its boundary points” and “$A$ contains some (not all) of its boundary points” are false. As we have seen, $A$ contains all its boundary points.

- Statement $\text{int}\,A\ne A$ is true. Since $A$ contains all of its boundary points, we must have $A-∂A⊊A.$ Therefore $\text{int}\,A\ne A.$

Therefore, the correct answer is $\text{int}\,A\ne A$ only.

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Identifying True Statements Regarding the Inverse Function Theorem

:question/answer-fields.:answer-field/key: $f$ is invertible in some neighborhood of $x=1$
${f}^{-1}(y)$ is continuously differentiable in a neighborhood of $y=-2$

questions.:question/problem:
![](images/0a/0a79260df29825684d6bdf6197df8581adf5a5a2d1d89938c299f18b3f33bf7c.png)

The function $f(x),$ whose graph is shown above, has a stationary point at $x=2$ and is continuously differentiable everywhere except at $x=3.$  By considering the points indicated in the diagram, determine which of the following statements **must** be true according to the inverse function theorem.

Select all that apply.
questions.:question/worked-solution:
The inverse function theorem for single-variable functions states the following:

*If $f:U\to R$ is continuously differentiable on an open set $U⊆R,$ $f(a)=b$ and ${f}^{′}(a)\ne 0$ for $a\in U,$ then*

- *$f$ is invertible in some neighborhood of $a,$*

- *${f}^{-1},$ the inverse of $f,$ is continuously differentiable in a neighborhood of $b,$ and*

- *the derivative of ${f}^{-1}$ is given by* 

$$
{({f}^{-1})}^{′}(b)=\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(a)}=\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(b))}\,.
$$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement “$f$ is invertible in some neighborhood of $x=1$” is true. The function $f$ satisfies the conditions for the inverse function theorem at $x=1.$ Indeed,

- $f$ is continuously differentiable on an open set containing $x=1,$ for example, $(0,2),$ and

- the derivative of $f$ is nonzero at $x=1,$ i.e., ${f}^{′}(1)\ne 0.$

Therefore, by the inverse function theorem, $f$ is invertible in *some* neighborhood of $x=1.$

- Statement “${f}^{-1}(y)$ is continuously differentiable in a neighborhood of $y=-2$” is false. Notice that $y=-2=f(2).$  However, the function $f$ does *not* satisfy the conditions for the inverse function theorem at $x=2$ since ${f}^{′}(2)=0.$ So, the theorem can't be applied in this situation.

- Statement “The derivative of ${f}^{-1}(y)$ at $y=2.91$ equals $\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(3)}$” is false. Notice that $y=2.91=f(3),$ but $f$ is not continuous at $x=3.$ So, the theorem can't be applied in this situation.

Therefore, the correct answer is “$f$ is invertible in some neighborhood of $x=1$” only.

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Classifying Local Extrema Using Sylvester's Criterion

questions.:question/problem:
The quadratic Taylor approximation of the function $f(x)$ about $x=a\in {R}^{2}$ is given by

$$
f(x)≈4+\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^{T}A(x-a),
$$

where 

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}5 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.
questions.:question/worked-solution:
The point $a\in {R}^{n}$ is a critical point of the function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ if ${f}^{′}(a)={0}^{T}.$ In such cases, we can classify $a$ as follows:

- if ${f}^{″}(a)$ is positive definite, then $a$ is a local minimum

- if ${f}^{″}(a)$ is negative definite, then $a$ is a local maximum

- if ${f}^{″}(a)$ is neither positive-definite nor negative-definite, then $a$ is a saddle point

In this case, we have $A={f}^{″}(a).$ Now, before we examine the statements, let's recall how to categorize quadratic forms.

Let ${Δ}_{i}$ for $i=1,2,…,n$  denote the leading principal minors of an $n\times n$ matrix $A.$ Then, according to Sylvester's criterion, the quadratic form ${x}^{T}\,A\,x$ (as well as the matrix $A$) is 

- positive-definite if and only if ${Δ}_{i}>0$ for all $i=1,2,…,n,$

- negative-definite if and only if, for all $i=1,2,…,n,$ we have ${Δ}_{i}<0$ when $i$ is odd, and ${Δ}_{i}>0$ when $i$ is even.

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn.

- Statement “${a}_{11}=5$ and $det(A)=2$” is false. Indeed, ${a}_{11}=5,$ but

$$
det(A)=|\begin{aligned}5 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}|=1.
$$

- Statement “$A$ is positive-definite” is true. Notice that

$$
\begin{aligned}{Δ}_{1} & ={a}_{11}=5>0, \\ {Δ}_{2} & =|\begin{aligned}5 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}|=1>0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, by Sylvester's criterion, the matrix $A$ is positive-definite.

- Statement “$a$ is a local minimum of $f$” is true. Since the matrix $A$ is positive-definite, the critical point $a$ is a local minimum of $f.$

Therefore, the correct answer is “$A$ is positive-definite”; “$a$ is a local minimum of $f$” only.

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Using the Second Derivative Test To Classify a Point on a Solution Curve

:question/answer-fields.:answer-field/key: $(-\frac{1}{2},1)$ is a stationary point of the function $f$
$(-\frac{1}{2},1)$ is a local maximum point of the function $f$
$(-\frac{1}{2},1)$ is an inflection point of the function $f$

questions.:question/problem:
The function $y=f(x)$ satisfies the differential equation 

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{y}{1+{x}^{2}}.
$$

Given that the point $(-\frac{1}{2},1)$ lies on the graph of $y=f(x),$ which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.
questions.:question/worked-solution:
First, we find the value of the first and second derivatives of the function at the given point.

To find the first derivative of $f$ at $(-\frac{1}{2},1),$ we substitute the coordinates of our point into the differential equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{(-1/2,1)} & ={\left(\frac{y}{1+{x}^{2}}\right)|}_{(-1/2,1)} \\  & =\frac{1}{1+{\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{4}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

To find the second derivative, we first need to differentiate the equation and then substitute the coordinates of the point:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\right) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}\left(\frac{y}{1+{x}^{2}}\right) \\  & =\frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-\frac{2xy}{(1+{x}^{2})^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}}\cdot \frac{y}{1+{x}^{2}}-\frac{2xy}{(1+{x}^{2})^{2}} \\  & =\frac{y(1-2x)}{(1+{x}^{2})^{2}} \\ {\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}|}_{(-1/2,1)} & ={\left(\frac{y(1-2x)}{(1+{x}^{2})^{2}}\right)|}_{(-1/2,1)} \\  & =\frac{1(1-2\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right))}{{(1+{\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)}^{2})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{32}{25}.\end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's examine the statements in turn.

- Statement “$(-\frac{1}{2},1)$ is a stationary point of the function $f$” is false. Indeed, since

$$
{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{(-1/2,1)}=\frac{4}{5}\ne 0,
$$

we obtain that $(-\frac{1}{2},1)$ is not a stationary point of the function $f.$

- Statement “$(-\frac{1}{2},1)$ is a local maximum point of the function $f$” is false. There is no critical point at $(-\frac{1}{2},1).$ Therefore we cannot have a local minimum at that point.

- Statement “$(-\frac{1}{2},1)$ is an inflection point of the function $f$” is false. Since the second derivative is not zero, there is no inflection point at $(-\frac{1}{2},1).$

Therefore, the correct answer is "None of those listed."

$$
\begin{aligned} & T\begin{bmatrix}kx \\ ky\end{bmatrix}=kT\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}, \\  & T\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}+{y}_{2}\end{bmatrix}=T\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {y}_{1}\end{bmatrix}+T\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{2} \\ {y}_{2}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Checking the first condition, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}T\begin{bmatrix}kx \\ ky\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}kx+ky \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}k(x+y) \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =k\begin{bmatrix}x+y \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =kT\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

- Checking the second condition, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}T\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}+{y}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}({x}_{1}+{x}_{2})+({y}_{1}+{y}_{2}) \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}({x}_{1}+{y}_{1})+({x}_{2}+{y}_{2}) \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1}+{y}_{1} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{2}+{y}_{2} \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =T\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {y}_{1}\end{bmatrix}+T\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{2} \\ {y}_{2}\end{bmatrix}.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{T}$ is a linear transformation.

As a result, all three statements are true.

questions.:question/problem:
Which of the following are mathematical predicates of one variable?

Select all that apply.
questions.:question/worked-solution:
A *predicate* of one variable is a sentence that contains the variable defined on some *universal set* and has the property that when we substitute any concrete value of the variable into the predicate, the result becomes a statement that is either true or false.

With that in mind, let's examine our options. 

- Option “$x$ is a negative number” is a predicate. Substituting a concrete value for $x$ into the sentence, we get a statement that is either true or false.

- Option “Why is $y$ an even number?” is *not* a predicate. Substituting a concrete value for $y$ into the sentence, we do not get a statement that is either true or false. Rather, it will give a question.

- Option ${z}^{2}-2$ is *not* a predicate. Substituting a concrete value for $z$ into the sentence, we do not get a statement that is either true or false.

Therefore, the correct answer is “$x$ is a negative number” only.

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Identifying the Orthogonality of a Two-Vector Set

questions.:question/problem:
$$
{u}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 3 \\ 5\end{bmatrix},\,{u}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 4 \\ -1\end{bmatrix},\,{u}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 3 \\ -3\end{bmatrix}
$$

Consider the vectors above, and let $Q$ be an orthogonal linear transformation. Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.
questions.:question/worked-solution:
Since $Q$ is orthogonal, we have that $Q(x)\cdot Q(y)=x\cdot y$ for any vectors $x$ and $y.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement ${u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=0$ is false since

$$
{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 3 \\ 5\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 4 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}=2+12-5=9\ne 0.
$$

- Statement “${Q({u}_{1}),Q({u}_{2}),Q({u}_{3})}$ is orthogonal” is false. Notice that, for example, $Q({u}_{1})⊥̸Q({u}_{2})$ since

$$
Q({u}_{1})\cdot Q({u}_{2})={u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}\ne 0.
$$

- Statement “${Q({u}_{1}),Q({u}_{2}),Q({u}_{3})}$ is orthonormal” is false since the set is not even orthogonal.

Therefore, the correct answer is "None of the statements are true."

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Identifying Orthogonal Matrices

questions.:question/problem:
$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}
$$

Consider the matrix $A$ above. Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.
questions.:question/worked-solution:
Recall that a square matrix $A$ is **orthogonal** if and only if

$$
A\cdot {A}^{T}={A}^{T}\cdot A=I
$$

where $I$ is the identity matrix.

With that in mind, let's examine the given statements. 

- Statement “$A$ is a square matrix” is false. The number of rows in $A$ is not the same as the number of columns. So, it's not a square matrix.

- Statement ${A}^{T}\cdot A=I$ is true. Note that

$$
{A}^{T}\cdot A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

- Statement “$A$ is an orthogonal matrix” is false. Since $A$ is not a square matrix, our matrix is **not** orthogonal.

Therefore, the correct answer is ${A}^{T}\cdot A=I$ only.

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Identifying the Orthogonality of a Two-Vector Set

questions.:question/problem:
$$
{u}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{4}{5} \\ \frac{3}{5}\end{bmatrix},\,{u}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{3}{5} \\ \frac{4}{5}\end{bmatrix}
$$

Consider the vectors above, and let $Q$ be an orthogonal linear transformation. Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.
questions.:question/worked-solution:
Since $Q$ is orthogonal, we have that $Q(x)\cdot Q(y)=x\cdot y$ for any vectors $x$ and $y.$

The linear transformation $Q$ being orthogonal is equivalent to the following:

- The matrix $Q$ of transformation $Q$ relative to any orthonormal basis (including the standard basis) of ${R}^{n}$ is orthogonal.

- $||Q(x)||=||x||.$

- If $x⊥y$ then $Q(x)⊥Q(y)$ for any $x,y\in {R}^{n}.$ In general, $Q$ preserves the angle between any two vectors.

- $Q$ maps any orthogonal (orthonormal) set into an orthogonal (orthonormal) set.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement ${u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=0$ is true. Indeed,

$$
{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{4}{5} \\ \frac{3}{5}\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}-\frac{3}{5} \\ \frac{4}{5}\end{bmatrix}=-\frac{12}{25}+\frac{12}{25}=0.
$$

- Statement “${Q({u}_{1}),Q({u}_{2})}$ is orthogonal” is true. Indeed, $Q({u}_{1})⊥Q({u}_{2})$ since

$$
Q({u}_{1})\cdot Q({u}_{2})={u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=0.
$$

- Statement “${Q({u}_{1}),Q({u}_{2})}$ is orthonormal” is true. Indeed, both $Q({u}_{1})$ and $Q({u}_{2})$ are unit vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}‖Q({u}_{1})‖ & =‖{u}_{1}‖=\sqrt{\left(\frac{4}{5}\right)^{2}+\left(\frac{3}{5}\right)^{2}}=1 \\ ‖Q({u}_{2})‖ & =‖{u}_{2}‖=\sqrt{\left(-\frac{3}{5}\right)^{2}+\left(\frac{4}{5}\right)^{2}}=1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is ${u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=0$; “${Q({u}_{1}),Q({u}_{2})}$ is orthogonal”; “${Q({u}_{1}),Q({u}_{2})}$ is orthonormal”.

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Cartesian Products With Three Sets

questions.:question/problem:
If $A=\{p,q\}$ and $B=\{2,4,6\},$ which of the following elements belong to $A\times A\times B?$

Select all that apply.
questions.:question/worked-solution:
The Cartesian product $A\times B\times C$ consists of all ordered triples whose first coordinate belongs to $A,$ second coordinate belongs to $B,$ and the third coordinate belongs to $C.$

In this case, $A\times A\times B$ consists of every combination of $\{p,q\}$ with $\{p,q\}$ and $\{2,4,6\},$ which results in

$$
\begin{aligned}A\times A\times B=\{ & (p,p,2),(p,p,4),(p,p,6),(p,q,2),(p,q,4),(p,q,6), \\  & (q,p,2),(q,p,4),(q,p,6),(q,q,2),(q,q,4),(q,q,6)\}.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that

$$
|A\times A\times B|=|A|\cdot |A|\cdot |B|=2\cdot 2\cdot 3=12.
$$

From the given options, we see that both $(p,q,2)$ and $(q,q,6)$ are in $A\times A\times B.$

Therefore, the correct answer is $(p,q,2)$; $(q,q,6)$ only.

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Classifying a Given Critical Point Using the Second Derivative Test

questions.:question/problem:
Consider the function $f(x)=2{x}^{3}-12{x}^{2}+24x.$ Given that ${f}^{′}(2)=0,$ which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.
questions.:question/worked-solution:
We're given that $x=2$ is a stationary point of $f(x).$ We will use the second derivative test to classify this stationary point.

Calculating the first derivative for the function $f(x)=2{x}^{3}-12{x}^{2}+24x,$ we get

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=6{x}^{2}-24x+24.
$$

Calculating the second derivative, we get 

$$
{f}^{″}(x)=12x-24.
$$

Substituting $x=2,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(2) & =12\cdot 2-24=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the second derivative is zero, we conclude that the test is inconclusive, we need to use the first derivative test.

Let's  find other stationary points. These points are the solution of the equation ${f}^{′}(x)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}6{x}^{2}-24x+24 & =0 \\ 6(x-2)^{2} & =0 \\ x & =2\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, the only stationary point is $x=2.$

Let's choose auxiliary points from each side of the stationary point and evaluate the first derivative at them. We take the auxiliary points $x=1,3$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(1) & =6(1)^{2}-24(1)+24=6>0 \\ {f}^{′}(3) & =6(3)^{2}-24(3)+24=6>0.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Since the first derivative does not change the sign at $x=2$, we conclude that $f(x)$ has no relative extrema at this point.

Therefore, the correct answer is ${f}^{″}(2)=0$ only.

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Finding Critical Points and Then Classifying Them Using the Second Derivative Test

questions.:question/problem:
For the function $f(x)=-3{x}^{5/2}+5{x}^{3/2}+15$ on $(0,\infty ),$ which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.
questions.:question/worked-solution:
We need to identify whether $x=1$ is a critical point. If it is, we then need to classify it using the second derivative test.

First, we need to identify the critical points. Differentiating $f(x)=-3{x}^{5/2}+5{x}^{3/2}+15,$ we get

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=-3\cdot \frac{5}{2}{x}^{3/2}+5\cdot \frac{3}{2}{x}^{1/2}=-\frac{15}{2}{x}^{3/2}+\frac{15}{2}{x}^{1/2},
$$

and solving ${f}^{′}(x)=0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{15}{2}{x}^{3/2}+\frac{15}{2}{x}^{1/2} & =0 \\ -\frac{15}{2}{x}^{1/2}(x-1) & =0 \\ x & =0,1.\end{aligned}
$$

So we have a critical point at $x=1.$

Next, we need to determine the sign of ${f}^{″}(x)$ at this critical point. Computing ${f}^{″}(x),$ we get

$$
{f}^{″}(x)=-\frac{15}{2}\cdot \frac{3}{2}{x}^{1/2}+\frac{15}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{2}{x}^{-1/2}=-\frac{45}{4}{x}^{1/2}+\frac{15}{4}{x}^{-1/2},
$$

and evaluating ${f}^{″}(x)$ at $x=1$, we get

$$
{f}^{″}(1)=-\frac{45}{4}(1)^{1/2}+\frac{15}{4}(1)^{-1/2}=-\frac{15}{2}<0.
$$

The second derivative is negative at $x=1,$ so this critical point is a relative *maximum*. 

Therefore, comparing our results with the given statements, we conclude that:

- $x=1$ is a critical point of $f(x)\,✓$

- ${f}^{″}(1)<0\,✓$

- $f(x)$ has a relative *maximum* at $x=1\,\times $

Therefore, the correct answer is “$x=1$ is a critical point of $f(x)$”; ${f}^{″}(1)<0$ only.

$$

and solving ${f}^{′}(x)=0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}15{x}^{4}-30{x}^{2} & =0 \\ 15{x}^{2}({x}^{2}-2) & =0 \\ 15{x}^{2}(x+\sqrt{2})(x-\sqrt{2}) & =0 \\ x & =\pm \sqrt{2},0.\end{aligned}
$$

So we have critical points at $x=\pm \sqrt{2},0.$ We're interested in the critical point $x=\sqrt{2}.$

Next, we need to determine the sign of ${f}^{″}(x)$ at this critical point. Computing ${f}^{″}(x),$ we get

$$
{f}^{″}(x)=60{x}^{3}-60x,
$$

and evaluating ${f}^{″}(x)$ at $x=\sqrt{2}$, we get

$$
{f}^{″}(\sqrt{2})=60(\sqrt{2})^{3}-60\sqrt{2}=60\sqrt{2}>0.
$$

The second derivative is positive at $x=\sqrt{2},$ so this critical point is a relative *minimum*. 

Therefore, comparing our results with the given statements, we conclude that:

- $x=\sqrt{2}$ is a critical point of $f(x)\,✓$

- ${f}^{″}(\sqrt{2})>0\,\times $

- $f(x)$ has a relative *minimum* at $x=\sqrt{2}\,✓$

questions.:question/problem:
Consider the function $f(x)=3{x}^{4}+4{x}^{3}-30{x}^{2}+36x+12.$ Given that ${f}^{′}(1)=0,$ which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.
questions.:question/worked-solution:
We're given that $x=1$ is a stationary point of $f(x).$ We will use the second derivative test to classify this stationary point.

Calculating the first derivative for the function $f(x)=3{x}^{4}+4{x}^{3}-30{x}^{2}+36x+12,$ we get

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=12{x}^{3}+12{x}^{2}-60x+36.
$$

Calculating the second derivative, we get 

$$
{f}^{″}(x)=36{x}^{2}+24x-60.
$$

Substituting $x=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(1) & =36(1)^{2}+24(1)-60=0\end{aligned}
$$

Since the second derivative is zero, we conclude that the test is inconclusive, we need to use the first derivative test.

Let's  find other stationary points. Solving ${f}^{′}(x)=0$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}12{x}^{3}+12{x}^{2}-60x+36 & =0 \\ 12({x}^{3}+{x}^{2}-5x+3) & =0 \\ 12(x-1)({x}^{2}+2x-3) & =0 \\ 12(x-1)(x-1)(x+3) & =0 \\ x & =-3,1.\end{aligned}
$$

 

So we have two stationary points, $x=-3$ and $x=1.$ Next, to determine whether these points are local maxima or minima, we use the first derivative test.

Let's choose the test points $x=-4,0,2$ and evaluate the first derivative at these points.

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(-4) & =12(-4-1)^{2}(-4+3)=-300<0 \\ {f}^{′}(0) & =12(0-1)^{2}(0+3)=36>0 \\ {f}^{′}(2) & =12(2-1)^{2}(2+3)=60>0\end{aligned}
$$

We summarize the information in a table, shown below.

| $x$ | $(-\infty ,-3)$ | $-3$ | $(-3,1)$ | $1$ | $(1,\infty )$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Test Point | $-4$ |  | $0$ |  | $2$ |
| ${f}^{′}$ | $-$ | $0$ | $+$ | $0$ | $+$ |
| $f$ | $↘$ | min | $↗$ |  | $↗$ |

At $x=1,$  the first derivative does not change the sign. Therefore, $x=1$ is neither a local minimum nor a local maximum.
Therefore, the correct answer is "None of the statements are true."

questions.:question/problem:
For the function $f(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x,$ which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.
questions.:question/worked-solution:
We need to identify whether $x=\frac{\pi }{4}$ is a critical point. If it is, we then need to classify it using the second derivative test.

First, we need to identify the critical points. Differentiating $f(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x,$ we get

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡x={cos}^{2}⁡x-{sin}^{2}⁡x=\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x),
$$

and solving ${f}^{′}(x)=0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x) & =0 \\ 2x & =\frac{\pi }{2}+n\pi , \\ x & =\frac{\pi }{4}+\frac{n\pi }{2},\end{aligned}
$$

where $n$ is an integer.

So we have critical points at $x=\frac{\pi }{4}+\frac{n\pi }{2}.$ We're interested in the critical point $x=\frac{\pi }{4}.$

Next, we need to determine the sign of ${f}^{″}(x)$ at this critical point. Computing ${f}^{″}(x),$ we get

$$
{f}^{″}(x)=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x),
$$

and evaluating ${f}^{″}(x)$ at $x=\frac{\pi }{4}$, we get

$$
{f}^{″}\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4})=-2<0.
$$

The second derivative is negative at $x=\frac{\pi }{4},$ so this critical point is a relative *maximum*. 

Therefore, comparing our results with the given statements, we conclude that:

- $x=\frac{\pi }{4}$ is a critical point of $f(x)\,✓$

- ${f}^{″}\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)<0\,✓$

- $f(x)$ has a relative *maximum* at $x=\frac{\pi }{4}\,\times $

Therefore, the correct answer is “$x=\frac{\pi }{4}$ is a critical point of $f(x)$”; ${f}^{″}\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)<0$ only.

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Finding the Intervals of Concavity of a Function

questions.:question/problem:
Consider the function $f(x)={x}^{2}-\frac{1}{x}$ defined on $x\in (0,\infty ).$ Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.
questions.:question/worked-solution:
First, we calculate the second derivative of $f(x),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =2x+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}} \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =2-\frac{2}{{x}^{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

To find where the function is concave up, we need to solve ${f}^{″}(x)>0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2-\frac{2}{{x}^{3}} & >0 \\ 2 & >\frac{2}{{x}^{3}} \\ {x}^{3} & >1 \\ x & >1\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we used the fact that $x>0.$

Hence, ${f}^{″}(x)>0$ when $x>1.$ So the graph is concave up on the interval $(1,\infty ).$

The function $f(x)$ is concave down when ${f}^{″}(x)<0.$ By similar reasoning to before, this leads to the inequality $2-\frac{2}{{x}^{3}}<0,$ which has the solution $(0,1).$

Therefore, the correct answer is " “$f(x)$ is concave down on $(0,1)$” only."

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Identifying Equations With Infinitely Many Solutions

questions.:question/problem:
Which of the following equations has infinitely many solutions?

Select all that apply.
questions.:question/worked-solution:
Let's attempt to solve each equation in turn:

- For the first equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}-3x+2 & =-3x+7 \\ -3x+2+3x & =-3x+7+3x \\ 2 & =7.\end{aligned}
$$

This equation is false for all values of $x.$

- For the second equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}6x+1 & =6x+5 \\ 6x+1-6x & =6x+5-6x \\ 1 & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

This equation is false for all values of $x.$

- For the third equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}7x-4 & =6x-6 \\ 7x-4-6x & =6x-6-6x \\ x-4 & =-6 \\ x-4+4 & =-6+4 \\ x & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation $7x-4=6x-6$ has the unique solution $x=-2.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "None."

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Applying the Linearity Principle to the Solutions of a Homogeneous System of ODEs

questions.:question/problem:
Suppose ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ are both solutions of the homogeneous system
${x}^{′}(t)=A\text{ }x(t).$
Which of the following is **always** a solution of the same system?

Select all that apply.
questions.:question/worked-solution:
The *linearity principle* for systems of linear ordinary differential equations (ODEs) states that if ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ are solutions to a homogeneous linear system, then for any constants ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2},$ the linear combination 

$$
{c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t)
$$

is also a solution of the system. 

With that in mind, let's examine the given expressions.

- Option $x(t)=2\cdot {x}_{1}(t)-{x}_{2}(t)$ is a solution to the system. Indeed, notice that

$$
2\cdot {x}_{1}(t)+(-1)\cdot {x}_{2}(t)
$$

is a linear combination of the solutions ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ with constant multiplies ${c}_{1}=2$ and ${c}_{2}=-1,$ respectively.

- Option $x(t)={x}_{1}(t)-t\cdot {x}_{2}(t)$ might be *not* a solution to the system since it's not a linear combination of the solutions ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t).$ Notice that the multiplier of the second term is not a constant.

- Option “$x(t)={x}_{1}(t)⊙{x}_{2}(t)$ (element-wise product)” might be *not* a solution to the system since it's not a linear combination of the solutions ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t).$

Therefore, the correct answer is $x(t)=2\cdot {x}_{1}(t)-{x}_{2}(t)$ only.

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Constructing General Solutions of First-Order Linear Systems of ODEs

questions.:question/problem:
Let ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ satisfy the homogeneous system ${x}^{′}(t)=A\text{ }x(t)$ and ${x}_{p}(t)$ satisfy the inhomogeneous system
${x}^{′}(t)=A\text{ }x(t)+f(t).$
Which of the following is **always** a solution of the same inhomogeneous system?

Select all that apply.
questions.:question/worked-solution:
Recall that if ${x}_{h}(t)$ satisfies a homogeneous linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)$ and ${x}_{p}(t)$ is a particular solution to an inhomogeneous linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+f(t),$ then ${x}_{h}(t)+{x}_{p}(t)$ is also a solution to the same inhomogeneous system.

Additonally, the *linearity principle* for systems of linear ordinary differential equations (ODEs) states that if ${x}_{1}(t),$ ${x}_{2}(t),…,{x}_{k}(t)$ are solutions to a homogeneous linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ then any linear combination 

$$
{c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t)+⋯+{c}_{k}{x}_{k}(t)
$$

with ${c}_{1},{c}_{2},…,{c}_{k}\in R$ is also a solution of the same homogeneous system. 

With that in mind, let's examine the given expression.

- Option ${x}_{1}(t)-{x}_{2}(t)$ might be *not* a solution to the inhomogeneous system. Notice that ${x}_{1}(t)-{x}_{2}(t)$ can't be written as 

$$
{x}_{h}(t)+{x}_{p}(t),
$$

where ${x}_{h}(t)$ is a solution of the homogeneous system, because it lacks the particular solution term ${x}_{p}(t).$

- Option $5\cdot {x}_{p}(t)$ might be *not* a solution to the inhomogeneous system. Notice that $5\cdot {x}_{p}(t)$ can't be written as 

$$
{x}_{h}(t)+{x}_{p}(t),
$$

where ${x}_{h}(t)$ is a solution of the homogeneous system, because of the multiplier $5$ next to the particular solution ${x}_{p}(t).$

- Option $-3\cdot {x}_{2}(t)-{x}_{p}(t)$ might be *not* a solution to the inhomogeneous system. Notice that $-3\cdot {x}_{2}(t)-{x}_{p}(t)$ can't be written as 

$$
{x}_{h}(t)+{x}_{p}(t),
$$

where ${x}_{h}(t)$ is a solution of the homogeneous system, because of the multiplier $-1$ next to the particular solution ${x}_{p}(t).$

Therefore, the correct answer is "None".

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Identifying a Decoupled System of Linear ODEs

questions.:question/problem:
Which of the following systems of linear ODEs are decoupled?

Select all that apply.
questions.:question/worked-solution:
A *decoupled system* consists of equations depending on only one variable, such as

$$
{x}_{i}^{′}(t)={\lambda }_{i}{x}_{i}(t),
$$

where ${\lambda }_{i}$ is a constant. This means that we can solve each equation independently. 

With this in mind, let's examine our systems.

- System $\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t) &=6{x}_{1}(t)-2{x}_{2}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t) &=4{x}_{1}(t)+3{x}_{2}(t)\end{aligned}\right.$ is *not* decoupled because some of its equations depend on more than one variable. For example, ${x}_{1}^{′}(t)=6{x}_{1}(t)-2{x}_{2}(t)$ depends on ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t).$

- System $\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t) &=5{x}_{1}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t) &=-8{x}_{2}(t)\end{aligned}\right.$ is decoupled since its equations depend on only one variable each. Indeed, ${x}_{1}^{′}(t)=5{x}_{1}(t)$ depends on only ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}^{′}(t)=-8{x}_{2}(t)$ depends on only ${x}_{2}(t).$

- System $\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t) &=2{x}_{2}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t) &=-{x}_{1}(t)+{x}_{2}(t)\end{aligned}\right.$ is *not* decoupled because some of its equations depend on more than one variable. For example, ${x}_{1}^{′}(t)=-{x}_{1}(t)+{x}_{2}(t)$ depends on ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t).$

Therefore, the correct answer is $\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t) &=5{x}_{1}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t) &=-8{x}_{2}(t)\end{aligned}\right.$ only.

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Determining Stability in Euler's Method

questions.:question/problem:
For which of the following values is Euler's method stable, given that $\lambda $ is the parameter of the test equation ${y}^{′}=-\lambda y$ with $y=y(x),y(0)=1,x\ge 0,\lambda >0,$ and step size $Δx?$  

*Hint: The stability function for Euler's method is given by* $R(\lambda Δx)=1-\lambda Δx.$

Select all that apply.
questions.:question/worked-solution:
A numerical method
${y}_{n+1}={y}_{n}+Δ{y}_{n}$
is stable for a given step size $Δx$ if, when applied to the test equation

$$
{y}^{′}=-\lambda y,\,y(0)=1,\,x\ge 0,\,\lambda >0,
$$

the numerical solution satisfies ${y}_{n}\to 0$ as $n\to \infty ,$ just like the exact solution.

For stability, we require that the following condition holds:

$$
\begin{aligned}|R(\lambda Δx)| & <1 \\ |1-\lambda Δx| & <1\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this gives

$$
0<\lambda Δx<2.
$$

This means that Euler's method is stable when applied to the test equation for values in the region $0<\lambda Δx<2.$ Of the given values:

- $\lambda Δx=0.4$ falls *within* the given region,

- $\lambda Δx=2.0$ falls *outside* of the given region,

- $\lambda Δx=2.4$ falls *outside* the given region, and

- $\lambda Δx=1.2$ falls *within* the given region.

Hence, Euler's method is stable for $\lambda Δx=0.4$ and $\lambda Δx=1.2$ only.

Therefore, the correct answer is $\lambda Δx=0.4$; $\lambda Δx=1.2$ only.

questions.:question/problem:
$$

$$

Consider the differential equation above. Which of the following statements are true?

questions.:question/worked-solution:
Recall that to determine whether $y(x)$ is a solution to the differential equation, we substitute $y$ and its derivatives into the equation. 

Let's check each statement in turn.

- Statement “${y}_{1}(x)={e}^{3x}$ is a solution to the equation” is false. We find the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{1}(x):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{1}^{′}(x) & =3{e}^{3x} \\ {y}_{1}^{″}(x) & =9{e}^{3x}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's substitute ${y}_{1}(x)$ and its derivatives into the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}9{e}^{3x}-3(3{e}^{3x})+2({e}^{3x}) & =0 \\ 8 & =0\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

So, ${y}_{1}(x)$ is not a solution to the equation.

where $R(\lambda Δx)$ is referred to as the stability function of the method. The set of values for which the method is stable, given by $|R(\lambda Δx)|<1,$ is called the stability region of the method.

The stability function of the implicit Euler method is

$$
R(\lambda Δx)=\frac{1}{1+\lambda Δx}.
$$

Let's check the stability of the Implicit Euler Method for each of the given values in turn.

- For $\lambda Δx=0.95,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|R(0.95)| & =|\frac{1}{1+0.95}| \\  & =|\frac{1}{1.95}| \\  & =0.5128…<1.\,✓\end{aligned}

$$

- For $\lambda Δx=0.4,$ we have

- For $\lambda Δx=2.3,$ we have

Let's check each statement in turn.

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{1}^{′}(x) & =3{e}^{3x} \\ {y}_{1}^{″}(x) & =9{e}^{3x}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's substitute ${y}_{1}(x)$ and its derivatives into the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}9{e}^{3x}-6\cdot 3{e}^{3x}+9{e}^{3x} & =0 \\ 0 & =0\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, ${y}_{1}(x)$ is a solution to the equation.

- Statement “${y}_{2}(x)={e}^{3x-1}$ is a solution to the equation” is true. First, we find the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{2}(x):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}^{′}(x) & =3{e}^{3x-1} \\ {y}_{2}^{″}(x) & =9{e}^{3x-1}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's substitute ${y}_{2}(x)$ and its derivatives into the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}9{e}^{3x-1}-6\cdot 3{e}^{3x-1}+9{e}^{3x-1} & =0 \\ 0 & =0\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, ${y}_{2}(x)$ is a solution to the equation.

- Statement “The functions ${y}_{1}(x)$ and ${y}_{2}(x)$ form a set of fundamental solutions to the equation” is false. Both ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ are solutions of the equation. To check if these functions are linearly independent, we compute the Wronskian:

$$
\begin{aligned}W({y}_{1},{y}_{2}) & =|\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & {y}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}^{′} & {y}_{2}^{′}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}{e}^{3x} & {e}^{3x-1} \\ 3{e}^{3x} & 3{e}^{3x-1}\end{aligned}| \\  & ={e}^{3x}\cdot 3{e}^{3x-1}-3{e}^{3x}\cdot {e}^{3x-1} \\  & =3{e}^{6x-1}-3{e}^{6x-1} \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Since the  Wronskian equals $0$ for all $x\in R,$ the functions are not linearly independent. Hence, ${y}_{1}(x)$ and ${y}_{2}(x)$ don't form a set of fundamental solutions to the equation.

questions.:question/worked-solution:
Recall that to determine whether $y(x)$ is a solution to the differential equation, we substitute $y$ and its derivatives into the equation. 

Let's check each statement in turn.

- Statement “${y}_{1}(x)={x}^{2}$ is a solution to the equation” is true. First, we find the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{1}(x):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{1}^{′}(x) & =2x \\ {y}_{1}^{″}(x) & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's substitute ${y}_{1}(x)$ and its derivatives into the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}\cdot 2-3x\cdot 2x+4{x}^{2} & =0 \\ 2{x}^{2}-6{x}^{2}+4{x}^{2} & =0 \\ 0 & =0\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, ${y}_{1}(x)$ is a solution to the equation.

- Statement “${y}_{2}(x)={x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)$ is a solution to the equation for $x>0.$” is true. First, we find the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{2}(x):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}^{′}(x) & =2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)+x \\ {y}_{2}^{″}(x) & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)+3\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's substitute ${y}_{2}(x)$ and its derivatives into the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}(2\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)+3)-3x(2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)+x)+4{x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x) & =0 \\ 2{x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)+3{x}^{2}-6{x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)-3{x}^{2}+4{x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x) & =0 \\ 0 & =0\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, ${y}_{2}(x)$ is a solution to the equation.

- Statement “The functions ${y}_{1}(x)$ and ${y}_{2}(x)$ form a set of fundamental solutions to the equation on $(0,\infty ).$” is true. Both ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ are solutions of the equation. To check if these functions are linearly independent, we compute the Wronskian:

$$
\begin{aligned}W({y}_{1},{y}_{2}) & =|\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & {y}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}^{′} & {y}_{2}^{′}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}{x}^{2} & {x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x) \\ 2x & 2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)+x\end{aligned}| \\  & ={x}^{2}(2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)+x)-{x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)\cdot 2x \\  & =2{x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)+{x}^{3}-2{x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x) \\  & ={x}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Since the  Wronskian is not identically $0$ on $(0,\infty ),$ the functions are linearly independent. Hence, ${y}_{1}(x)$ and ${y}_{2}(x)$ form a set of fundamental solutions to the equation on $(0,\infty ).$

Therefore, the correct answer is “${y}_{1}(x)={x}^{2}$ is a solution to the equation”; “${y}_{2}(x)={x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)$ is a solution to the equation for $x>0.$”; “The functions ${y}_{1}(x)$ and ${y}_{2}(x)$ form a set of fundamental solutions to the equation on $(0,\infty ).$”.

questions.:question/problem:
For which of the following functions is it valid to differentiate under the integral sign?

Select all that apply.
questions.:question/worked-solution:
Suppose $f(x,t)$ is continuous on $R=[a,b]\times [c,d]$ and $\frac{∂f}{∂t}$ exists and is continuous on $R.$ Then, the function

$$
F(t)={\int }_{a}^{b}f(x,t)\,\text{d}x
$$

is differentiable on $(c,d),$ and

$$
{F}^{′}(t)=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x,t)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{a}^{b}\frac{∂f}{∂t}(x,t)\,\text{d}x.
$$

This is known as *differentiating under the integral sign.*

With that in mind, let's check each function:

- For the first function, we have 

$$
{f}_{1}(x,t)=\frac{1}{\sqrt[3]{|x-t|}}.
$$

We fix ${t}_{0}\in (0,1)$ and choose $c<{t}_{0}<d$ such that $[c,d]⊆(0,1),$ so $R=[0,1]\times [c,d].$

Note that ${f}_{1}$ is undefined when $x=t,$ since the denominator vanishes. Thus, ${f}_{1}$ is not continuous on $R,$ and differentiating under the integral sign is *not* valid.

- For the second function, we have 

$$
{f}_{2}(x,t)=\frac{x}{1+{t}^{2}}.
$$

We fix ${t}_{0}\in R$ and choose $c<{t}_{0}<d,$ so $R=[0,1]\times [c,d].$

Note that ${f}_{2}$ is continuous on $R.$ Computing the partial derivative, we have

$$
\frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂t}=-\frac{2tx}{(1+{t}^{2})^{2}}
$$

which exists and is continuous on $R.$ Thus, differentiating under the integral sign is valid at ${t}_{0}.$ And since our choice of ${t}_{0}$ was arbitrary, we can compute ${F}_{2}^{′}(t)$ for all real $t.$

- For the third function, we have 

$$
{f}_{3}(x,t)=\frac{1}{1+x+t}.
$$

We fix ${t}_{0}\in (0,1)$ and choose $c<{t}_{0}<d$ such that $[c,d]⊂(0,1),$ so $R=[0,1]\times [c,d].$

Note that ${f}_{3}$ is continuous on $R$ (since the denominator never vanishes on $R$). Computing the partial derivative, we have

$$
\frac{∂{f}_{3}}{∂t}=-\frac{1}{(1+x+t)^{2}}
$$

which exists and is continuous on $R.$ Thus, differentiating under the integral sign is valid at ${t}_{0}.$ And since our choice of ${t}_{0}$ was arbitrary, we can compute ${F}_{3}^{′}(t)$ for all $t\in (0,1).$

Therefore, the correct answer is ${F}_{2}(t)={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{x}{1+{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}x,\,t\in R$; ${F}_{3}(t)={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{1+x+t}\,\text{d}x,\,t\in (0,1)$ only.

questions.:question/problem:
![](images/96/96df34b3f844ee5abace182769011a3b4b2e413100fbca4cf25e829ca67948cc.png)

Consider the phase line shown above. Which of the following differential equations could have this phase line?

Select all that apply.
questions.:question/worked-solution:
First, notice that all three differential equations are of the form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=f(y).
$$

The phase line gives us the following information:

- The equilibrium solutions are $y=2,$ $y=4$ and $y=6.$

- $f(y)$ is positive for $y\in (-\infty ,2)\cup (2,4)\cup (6,\infty ).$

- $f(y)$ is negative for $y\in (4,6).$

With this in mind, let's study each of the given equations.

- We start by considering

$$
{y}^{′}=(y-2)^{2}(y-4).
$$

In this case, $f(y)=(y-2)^{2}(y-4),$ and the equilibrium solutions are $y=2,4$ only.

Therefore, equation $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=(y-2)^{2}(y-4)$ does not have the given phase line.

- Next, we consider

$$
{y}^{′}=(y-2)(y-4)(y-6).
$$

In this case, $f(y)=(y-2)(y-4)(y-6),$ and the equilibrium solutions are $y=2,4,6.$

However, we note that $f(y)<0$ for $y\in (-\infty ,2).$ This does not correspond to the arrows shown on the phase line.

Therefore, equation $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=(y-2)(y-4)(y-6)$ does not have the given phase line.

- Finally, we consider ${y}^{′}=(y-2)^{2}(y-4)(y-6).$

First, we see that $f(y)=(y-2)^{2}(y-4)(y-6),$ so $f(y)=0$ if $y=2,4,6.$ So, the equilibrium solutions correspond to those shown in the phase line.

Now, we can construct a sign table for $f(y)$ as follows:

|  | $(-\infty ,2)$ | $(2,4)$ | $(4,6)$ | $(6,\infty )$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $(y-2)^{2}$ | $+$ | $+$ | $+$ | $+$ |
| $y-4$ | $-$ | $-$ | $+$ | $+$ |
| $y-6$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | $+$ |
| $f(y)$ | $+$ | $+$ | $-$ | $+$ |

So, we have that $f(y)$ is negative for $y\in (4,6),$ and $f(y)$ is positive for $y\in (-\infty ,2)\cup (2,4)\cup (6,\infty ).$
Therefore, equation $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=(y-2)^{2}(y-4)(y-6)$ has the given phase line.

Therefore, the correct answer is $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=(y-2)^{2}(y-4)(y-6)$ only.

questions.:question/problem:
Which of the following are linear differential operators?

Select all that apply.
questions.:question/worked-solution:
An $n$th-order differential operator $L$ is linear if it is of the following form:

$$
L(y)={f}_{n}(x)\frac{{\text{d}}^{n}y}{\text{d}{x}^{n}}+{f}_{n-1}(x)\frac{{\text{d}}^{n-1}y}{\text{d}{x}^{n-1}}+⋯+{f}_{1}(x)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+{f}_{0}(x)y
$$

where each ${f}_{i}$ is a function of $x$ only. 

With that in mind, let's check each operator.

- Operator ${D}_{1}$ is linear. It is a first-order linear differential operator of the form

$$
{D}_{1}(y)={f}_{1}(x)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+{f}_{0}(x)y
$$

with ${f}_{1}(x)=x-1$ and ${f}_{0}(x)=2x.$

- Operator ${D}_{2}$ is *not* linear. The coefficient of the first term is $y,$ which depends on $y$ and therefore fails linearity.

- Operator ${D}_{3}$ is linear. It is a third-order linear differential operator of the form

$$
{D}_{3}(y)={f}_{3}(x)\frac{{\text{d}}^{3}y}{\text{d}{x}^{3}}+{f}_{2}(x)\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+{f}_{1}(x)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+{f}_{0}(x)y
$$

with ${f}_{3}(x)=4,{f}_{2}(x)=0,{f}_{1}(x)=-{x}^{2},$ and ${f}_{0}(x)=x.$

Therefore, the correct answer is ${D}_{1}(y)=(x-1)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2xy$; ${D}_{3}(y)=4\frac{{\text{d}}^{3}y}{\text{d}{x}^{3}}-{x}^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+xy$ only.

is *homogeneous* when $f≡0,$ and *inhomogeneous* when $f≢0.$

questions.:question/problem:
Which of the following systems are homogeneous?

questions.:question/worked-solution:
Recall that a first-order linear system of differential equations with two dependent variables is a system of the form

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t) &=a(t){x}_{1}(t)+b(t){x}_{2}(t)+f(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t) &=c(t){x}_{1}(t)+d(t){x}_{2}(t)+g(t).\end{aligned}\right.
$$

If $f≡0$ and $g≡0$ (i.e., both $f$ and $g$ are zero functions), then the system is *homogeneous*. Otherwise, if at least one of $f$ or $g$ is not identically zero, the system is *inhomogeneous*.

With this in mind, let's inspect each system:

- System $\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t) &=-2{x}_{1}(t)+{x}_{2}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t) &=4{x}_{1}(t)-{x}_{2}(t)\end{aligned}\right.$ is homogeneous since it can be written in the standard form with $f≡0$ and $g≡0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t)=-2, &  & b(t)=1, &  & f(t)=0 \\ c(t)=4, &  & d(t)=-1, &  & g(t)=0\end{aligned}
$$

- System $\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t) &={x}_{1}(t)+2{x}_{2}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t) &=-{x}_{1}(t)+t\end{aligned}\right.$ is inhomogeneous since it can be written in the standard form with $g≢0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t)=1, &  & b(t)=2, &  & f(t)=0 \\ c(t)=-1, &  & d(t)=0, &  & g(t)=t\end{aligned}
$$

- System $\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t) &={x}_{2}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t) &=-{x}_{1}(t)\end{aligned}\right.$ is homogeneous since it can be written in the standard form with $f≡0$ and $g≡0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t)=0, &  & b(t)=1, &  & f(t)=0 \\ c(t)=-1, &  & d(t)=0, &  & g(t)=0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is $\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t) &=-2{x}_{1}(t)+{x}_{2}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t) &=4{x}_{1}(t)-{x}_{2}(t)\end{aligned}\right.$; $\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t) &={x}_{2}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t) &=-{x}_{1}(t)\end{aligned}\right.$ only.
